questions.q: Why does the lesson say a model can be 'fully up, fast, and error-free' and still be having an incident?
options: Because categories like biased output, drift-driven errors, and data leakage through responses don't necessarily trip a standard uptime or error-rate alert
Because uptime monitoring is always broken for AI systems
Because AI models are never actually monitored
Because incidents can only happen during scheduled maintenance windows
questions.explain: The lesson's key point is that several real AI incident categories can occur while every standard uptime/error dashboard still looks green.

questions.q: What are the five steps in the AI incident response sequence the lesson describes?
options: Detect, contain, assess impact via lineage, notify, remediate
Ignore, deny, escalate, blame, close the ticket
Retrain, redeploy, re-approve, relaunch, repeat
Only one step: immediately delete the model
questions.explain: The lesson lists this exact five-step sequence, adapted from standard security incident response with AI-specific detail at each stage.

questions.q: Why does the lesson call a model's registry alias the 'AI-specific kill switch'?
options: Moving the alias back to a last known-good version is often a single operation that contains harm without a code deployment or release cycle
It permanently deletes the model and all its data
It automatically notifies regulators without any human involvement
It is a feature unique to generative AI systems only
questions.explain: The lesson frames alias rollback as the fastest containment action specifically because it requires no code deployment — just pointing the alias at a prior version.

questions.q: What precondition does the lesson say is required for alias rollback to actually work as a fast containment step?
options: Versioning and the registry must already be disciplined before the incident, so there's a clean version history to roll back to
The incident must be reported by an external auditor first
The model must be retrained from scratch during the incident
No precondition is needed — it always works regardless of prior practice
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly notes rollback isn't a capability you can retrofit mid-incident — it depends on the versioning and registry discipline from earlier lessons already being in place.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what should happen after an incident is contained, besides fixing the immediate cause?
options: Update the model card, feed the finding back into the approval process, and record the full incident in version history
Nothing further is needed once the immediate harm stops
Immediately delete all records of the incident to avoid liability
Automatically approve the next version without any review
questions.explain: The lesson stresses that containment alone isn't enough — the model card, approval process, and version history all need to capture what was learned.
